beats.beat: Judith tells Rowe she means to correct the story to the whole parish, whatever it costs her pride to explain a cracked wheel to fools.
Rowe says he does not want the rumour corrected so much as made true, and asks her, without any of Mrs Pike's staging, whether she would have him.
Wary of being a convenience to a story rather than a choice, Judith asks whether he asks from feeling or from wanting to stop tongues.

He answers with the sermon and the novels, admitting he has thought of her correcting him at the counter far more often than a man ought to think of someone he claims to dislike, and she laughs and lets it settle the matter.
They walk back into Amberlight together in full daylight this time, meaning to be seen.

turn.note: The engagement is decided, which resets what chapter 8 has to report to the parish.

problems: "which is the nearest thing to putting down a shield that a curate can manage" edges from free indirect discourse into narratorial commentary explaining the gesture's meaning rather than letting it stand.

listenability: The bracketed stage direction ['tag': '[quietly]'] on Rowe's line "Judith." is a format not used elsewhere in the series and risks being read aloud literally by narration; render it as prose instead, e.g. 'said Rowe, quietly.'

"I have wanted to go back and take it, and read the six, and come and tell you what I thought of them" stacks three coordinated infinitive actions in one breath inside emotional dialogue; split after 'take it' so the listener isn't carrying three verbs at once.
trope_note: Enemies of manner pays off straight here with the sermon/novels reconciliation; the chaperone's-absence consequence resolves through Judith's own correction rather than rescue, which is consistent with her established character.
fixes: Rewrite the '[quietly]' tag on Rowe's 'Judith.' line as ordinary narration rather than a bracketed stage direction.
Split 'I have wanted to go back and take it, and read the six, and come and tell you what I thought of them' after the first infinitive phrase.

Trim Rowe's long speech beginning 'I have gone over that half minute' by cutting the 'Tidiness would have been Miss Marchmont' sentence, which restates a joke chapter 3 already made, to bring the chapter closer to its target length.
Consider giving the 'shield' aside to Judith's perspective instead of narrator commentary, or cut it, to keep the free indirect voice consistent.

writer_note:
This story is now read by a single narrator rather than a
cast with a voice each, so the prose has to carry who is speaking. It was
written under the old rule, which forbade attribution because the voices made it
redundant.

Go through the chapter and add attribution wherever a listener — who cannot see
the page, and cannot look back — would lose track of who is speaking. A tag
belongs in its own narrator segment: `said Mrs Pike`, `Rowe said`, or an action
that does the same work: *Rowe turned the note over.* Two people alternating in
a plain exchange do not need one every line; the third turn usually does, and so
does every return to dialogue after narration, and every line in a scene of
three or more.

Do not attribute every line. An unbroken column of `said X` is padding, and it
is the opposite failure.

Where a line would be misread without it, you may add a `tag` to that segment —
`"[quietly]"`, `"[a beat]"`, `"[warmly]"` — as performance direction for the
voice. It is never printed and never spoken. A few a chapter at most, and never
to imitate a different person: one voice reads everyone.

Come back no longer than you started. These chapters are already at or over
their word ceiling, and attribution adds words — so take them back out of
restatement: a line of dialogue that lands followed by narration explaining that
it landed, a room established twice. If you come back long the check sends the
chapter straight back to be cut, which spends a revision on arithmetic instead
of on the prose.

Change nothing else. Same events, same beats, same jokes, same last line.
